title: Furnaces: Why we still burn fuel to heat our homes
summary: Explains why gas furnaces beat electric resistance heat on fuel use and cost, and introduces heat pumps as a far more efficient electric option that loses output below freezing.

assertions.quote: And that means that gas heat is a lot cheaper than electric heat

verdicts.note: US residential gas costs roughly a third to a quarter of electricity per unit of energy.
At 2024 US average residential prices electricity costs $48.30/MMBtu versus $14.00 for gas, a ratio of 3.45 (state range 1.69 Florida to 6.42 Alaska).

RMI's 2017-18 rate table puts Chicago at $0.111/kWh for electricity and $0.56/therm for gas (about $0.019/kWh), and Providence at $0.19/kWh and $1.23/therm (about $0.042/kWh), so gas was roughly 4.5-6 times cheaper per unit of energy.

Background statement that propane, oil and electricity have traditionally been significantly more expensive than natural gas for heating; not a measurement, and per raw energy unit rather than per delivered heat.
In the UK in June 2024, Octopus's average electricity unit rate was £0.2450/kWh against £0.0604/kWh for gas, about four times as much; government retail prices show similar gaps.

assertions.quote: air conditioners actually move three to four times as much energy than they consume.
A heat pump is essentially a modified air conditioner that is able to operate in reverse.
But along with getting less efficient, their actual heat output also drops.
Right now they don't work so well in climates like mine because when the temperature outside drops below freezing

verdicts.note: Cold-climate heat pumps are used widely in Maine, Canada and Scandinavia and keep delivering heat well below 0°F.
Over 25,000 products on the NEEP cold-climate list keep a COP of 2 or more at full capacity at 5F, and modelled per-household GHG savings are generally higher in cold climates.
RMI notes that hundreds of models operate efficiently at 5F and some heat at -13F, and it models cold-climate heat pumps heating homes in Chicago and Providence.
In monitored Minnesota homes cold-climate ASHPs cut heating costs 30-56%; cold weather raised backup and defrost use and lowered heat pump performance but overall system efficiencies remained high.
Across two New England winters, metered mini-splits kept heating below 0 F with average COP about 1.5 at -10 to 0 F, which the report calls far superior to resistance heat.
Prototype cold-climate heat pumps in occupied northern US and Canadian homes kept a median COP of 1.9 at 0-5 F, with most units above the ENERGY STAR 1.75 threshold in the field.

Standard heat pumps perform well to -8 to -10°C and cold-climate models to -25°C; Norway, with temperatures similar to Canada's, leads the world in heat pump penetration, with confirmed real-world performance there.
In 78 metered Maine homes with whole-home heat pump systems, the heat pumps provided over 70% of total heating needs, with wood 10% and fossil fuel 19%.

assertions.quote: If you’re installing an air conditioner, you might as well spend the extra dollars and make it a heat pump.

verdicts.note: Wholesale heat pumps cost only $200-$500 more than equivalent ACs, but heat pumps sized to fully electrify heating often cost more to install than AC plus furnace because of larger capacity, wiring and panel upgrades.

Edwards' national installed-cost medians put a heat pump at $6,185 against $4,684 for a central AC of the same 36,000 BTU/h size, so it adds heating for about $1,500 (roughly 30%) more, which is modest but not trivial.
Database costs put an efficient heat pump only about $370 above an equally efficient central AC ($5,550 vs $5,180), adding heating for little extra cost.

assertions.quote: a heat pump can move more heat energy into a living space than the natural gas itself contains

verdicts.note: Average lifetime GHG savings are positive in every state for every heat pump and grid scenario, including the conservative high-renewable-cost grid, though these are 2022-2038 long-run marginal grid factors rather than today's grid.
Heat pump adoption raises CO2 for only 2.1% of US houses, though the model assumes grid emissions fall 45% over the heat pump's life.

On 2016 short-term marginal grid data, heat pumps cut emissions versus gas in Oakland, Houston and Providence but raised them in coal-heavy Chicago (about 50% more), so the claim holds on most grids but not all.

LBNL: fuel switching boosted carbon cuts (68% vs 50%) in the electrification cluster, but those projects were mostly in states with low-carbon grids, and the authors expect lower carbon savings where electricity is more carbon-intensive.

On the 2024 UK grid, replacing a gas boiler with a heat pump cut household energy CO2eq by about 1.16 t/yr, 36% of the pre-adoption footprint, from measured consumption changes and government emission factors.
Even on relatively emissions-intensive electricity, heat pumps emit 20 to 30% less than gas furnaces (citing IEA 2022 and a consultancy), and near zero on clean grids.
Heat pump adoption raises CO2 for only 2.1% of US houses (1.7 million), but the estimate assumes grid CO2 emissions fall 45% over the heat pump's 15-year life.

Average GHG savings are positive in every state for every heat pump and future grid scenario, even the conservative high-renewable-cost one, with emissions levelized over a 16-year equipment lifetime (projected grids, not today's).

Using quarterly emission factors for the German grid, the measured heat pumps emitted on average 64 percent less CO2 in 2024 than gas heating; a calculation on measured efficiency, reported in a press release.
